title: Rice Leaf Yellowing (Nitrogen Deficiency)
content:
Why are my rice leaves turning yellow?

Yellow rice leaves often mean nitrogen deficiency, especially when older leaves turn pale first. Check your fertilizer schedule and apply nitrogen as recommended for your area. If unsure, ask a local agriculture officer before applying more fertilizer.

Symptoms: yellow leaves, pale older leaves

Possible causes: nitrogen deficiency

Solution: Check fertilizer schedule. Apply nitrogen as locally recommended. Avoid overwatering after application.

title: Rice Brown Spot Disease
content:
My rice has brown spots on the leaves. What should I do?

Brown spots on rice leaves can be brown spot disease, often worse when plants are nutrient-stressed. Improve drainage, avoid overcrowding, and use balanced fertilizer. Severely damaged leaves can be removed. Seek local advice if spots spread quickly.

Symptoms: brown spots on leaves, leaf tip burn

Possible causes: brown spot fungus, nutrient imbalance

Solution: Improve field drainage. Avoid dense planting. Use balanced fertilizer. Remove heavily infected leaves if practical.

title: Rice Blast Disease
content:
What causes rice blast and how do I manage it?

Rice blast often shows diamond-shaped lesions on leaves and can damage the neck of the panicle. Reduce excess nitrogen, manage water carefully, and prefer resistant varieties. For chemical control, follow only locally approved recommendations.

Symptoms: diamond-shaped lesions, leaf blight, neck rot

Possible causes: rice blast fungus

Solution: Use resistant varieties if available. Avoid excess nitrogen. Keep good water management. Ask local extension for approved fungicide guidance.

title: Rice Stem Borer
content:
Rice plants have dead hearts. Is it stem borer?

Dead hearts and white heads in rice often indicate stem borer damage. Remove heavily infested tillers, avoid staggered planting that keeps pests active, and protect beneficial insects. Use pesticides only if local guidance says the infestation is above threshold.

Symptoms: dead hearts, white heads, bored stems

Possible causes: stem borer insects

Solution: Remove and destroy infested tillers. Avoid staggered planting nearby. Encourage natural enemies. Use local threshold-based control advice.

title: Tomato Leaf Curl
content:
Tomato leaves are curling upward. What is wrong?

Upward curling and stunting in tomatoes can be leaf curl virus, often spread by whiteflies. Remove badly infected plants, reduce whitefly pressure, and avoid introducing infected seedlings. There is no simple cure once plants are infected.

Symptoms: upward leaf curl, stunted growth, yellowing

Possible causes: tomato leaf curl virus, whiteflies

Solution: Control whiteflies with nets or approved methods. Remove heavily infected plants. Avoid moving infected seedlings between fields.

title: Tomato Early Blight
content:
Tomato lower leaves have target-like brown spots.

Target-like brown spots on older tomato leaves often point to early blight. Remove infected lower leaves, water the soil rather than the foliage, and improve airflow. Rotate crops in the next season to reduce disease carryover.

Symptoms: target-like brown spots, lower leaf yellowing

Possible causes: early blight fungus

Solution: Improve air flow. Water at soil level. Remove infected lower leaves. Rotate crops next season.

title: Tomato Blossom End Rot
content:
Why do my tomatoes rot at the bottom of the fruit?

A dark sunken patch at the blossom end is usually blossom-end rot, linked to calcium uptake and uneven watering. Keep soil moisture steady, mulch the bed, and avoid heavy nitrogen that pushes soft growth.

Symptoms: dark sunken patch at fruit bottom

Possible causes: calcium imbalance, uneven watering

Solution: Keep soil moisture steady. Avoid extreme dry-wet cycles. Do not overapply nitrogen. Mulch to hold moisture.

title: Chili Aphid Infestation
content:
Chili leaves are curled and sticky. What pest is it?

Curled sticky chili leaves often mean aphids. Check the underside of leaves, rinse light infestations with water, and protect beneficial insects. Use soap sprays carefully and avoid harsh chemicals unless the infestation is severe.

Symptoms: curled leaves, sticky honeydew, ants on plant

Possible causes: aphids

Solution: Wash small infestations with water. Encourage ladybugs. Use mild soap spray carefully. Check underside of leaves often.

title: Chili Leaf Spot Disease
content:
Chili plants are dropping leaves with spots.

Leaf spots and drop on chili can be fungal or bacterial. Avoid watering from above, remove diseased leaves, and give plants more space for airflow. Clean tools so the problem does not spread.

Symptoms: circular leaf spots, leaf drop

Possible causes: fungal or bacterial leaf spot

Solution: Avoid overhead watering. Remove diseased leaves. Improve spacing and airflow. Clean tools between plants.

title: Cabbage Diamondback Moth
content:
Something is making holes in my cabbage leaves.

Holes in cabbage leaves are often caused by diamondback moth larvae. Scout often, handpick when numbers are low, protect seedbeds with nets, and rotate brassica crops to break the pest cycle.

Symptoms: holes in leaves, tiny green larvae

Possible causes: diamondback moth

Solution: Scout leaves regularly. Handpick larvae when few. Use nets on seedbeds. Rotate brassica crops.

title: Eggplant Fruit Borer
content:
Eggplant fruits have holes. What should I do?

Holes in eggplant fruit often mean fruit borer. Collect and destroy bored fruits, stake plants so you can inspect them easily, and do not leave fallen fruit in the field where pests continue breeding.

Symptoms: holes in fruit, frass near entry

Possible causes: fruit and shoot borer

Solution: Remove and destroy bored fruits. Stake plants for easier scouting. Avoid leaving fallen fruit in the field.

title: Onion Purple Blotch
content:
Onion leaves have purple lesions. Is that disease?

Purple lesions and tip dieback on onion leaves can be purple blotch. Reduce leaf wetness, improve drainage and spacing, and clear infected debris after harvest to lower next-season risk.

Symptoms: purple lesions on leaves, tip dieback

Possible causes: purple blotch fungus

Solution: Avoid overhead irrigation. Improve drainage. Do not overcrowd. Remove infected debris after harvest.

title: Maize Fall Armyworm
content:
My maize has larvae in the whorl and leaf damage.

Larvae in the maize whorl with windowpane leaf damage often indicate fall armyworm. Scout early, crush small numbers by hand, keep the field clean, and spray only when local guidance says the infestation is above threshold.

Symptoms: windowpane feeding, larvae in whorl, frass

Possible causes: fall armyworm

Solution: Scout whorls early morning. Crush larvae when few. Maintain field hygiene. Follow local threshold advice before spraying.

title: Maize Leaf Yellowing (Nitrogen Deficiency)
content:
Maize leaves show yellow V shapes from the tip.

A yellow V from the leaf tip on maize commonly signals nitrogen deficiency. Side-dress nitrogen at the recommended growth stage, control weeds, and avoid waterlogged soil that stresses roots.

Symptoms: V-shaped yellowing from leaf tip, pale plants

Possible causes: nitrogen deficiency

Solution: Side-dress nitrogen at recommended stage. Keep weeds down so they do not compete. Avoid waterlogging.

title: Bean Rust
content:
Bean leaves have rusty spots underneath.

Rusty pustules under bean leaves are often bean rust. Prefer resistant varieties, avoid handling wet plants, remove badly infected leaves, and rotate legumes to reduce disease buildup.

Symptoms: rusty pustules under leaves, yellowing

Possible causes: bean rust fungus

Solution: Choose resistant varieties if available. Avoid working plants when wet. Remove badly infected leaves. Rotate legumes.

title: Overwatering — Yellow Leaves
content:
Plants wilt even though the soil is wet. Why?

Wilting in wet soil often means roots are stressed from overwatering or poor drainage. Allow the top soil to dry a little between irrigations, improve drainage, and water in the morning so foliage dries faster.

Symptoms: yellow soft leaves, soggy soil, wilting despite wet soil

Possible causes: overwatering, poor drainage

Solution: Let soil dry slightly between irrigations. Improve drainage. Water in the morning. Check root health if plants decline.

title: Underwatering — Wilting Plants
content:
How often should I water vegetable beds in hot weather?

In hot weather, water deeply less often rather than light daily sprinkles. Mulch to hold moisture and irrigate early morning. Watch for dry soil and midday wilt that recovers overnight as signs plants need more water.

Symptoms: dry soil, leaf curling, midday wilt that recovers overnight

Possible causes: underwatering

Solution: Water deeply but less often. Mulch to reduce evaporation. Water early morning. Adjust schedule in hot weather.

title: NPK Fertilizer Basics
content:
What does NPK mean for fertilizer?

N supports leafy growth, P supports roots and flowering, and K supports overall strength and stress tolerance. Use amounts suited to the crop stage, prefer split applications, and stop if leaves show fertilizer burn.

Symptoms: slow growth, pale leaves, weak stems

Possible causes: nutrient imbalance

Solution: Use balanced fertilizer based on crop stage. Do not apply more after seeing leaf burn. Prefer split applications.

title: Fertilizer Leaf Burn
content:
Leaves burned after I fertilized. What happened?

Brown edges after fertilizing often mean salt burn from too much fertilizer or application against the stem. If drainage is good, gently flush the soil with water and use a lower dose next time.

Symptoms: brown leaf edges after fertilizing, white crust on soil

Possible causes: excess fertilizer, salt burn

Solution: Flush soil gently with clean water if drainage is good. Reduce next dose. Never place fertilizer against stems.

title: Composting Basics
content:
How can compost help my farm soil?

Well-rotted compost improves soil structure, moisture holding, and nutrient supply. Mix it into the topsoil before planting. Keep compost piles moist and turned so they break down evenly.

Symptoms: poor soil structure, low organic matter

Possible causes: lack of organic matter

Solution: Add well-rotted compost before planting. Mix into topsoil. Keep compost moist and aerated while making it.

title: Mulching Benefits
content:
Should I mulch vegetable beds?

Yes. Mulch slows drying, reduces weeds, and protects soil. Keep mulch slightly away from stems to avoid rot, and replenish it as it breaks down.

Symptoms: fast soil drying, many weeds

Possible causes: exposed soil

Solution: Apply organic mulch around plants. Keep mulch a little away from stems. Replenish as it breaks down.

title: Seedling Damping-off
content:
My seedlings fall over and die suddenly.

Sudden collapse at the soil line is often damping-off. Use clean trays, avoid overwatering, improve airflow, and discard infected seedlings so the fungus does not spread.

Symptoms: seedlings collapse at soil line, fuzzy mold

Possible causes: damping-off fungi

Solution: Use clean trays and well-drained media. Avoid overwatering. Give light airflow. Discard infected seedlings.

title: Early Pest Scouting
content:
How do I catch pest problems early?

Scout fields a few times each week. Look under leaves and at young shoots. Early detection lets you handpick or use milder methods before damage becomes severe.

Symptoms: unexpected crop damage

Possible causes: missed early pest signs

Solution: Walk fields 2-3 times a week. Check leaf undersides and growing tips. Act early when pests are few.

title: Pesticide Safety Guidelines
content:
When should I use pesticide on crops?

Use pesticides only when scouting shows high pressure and local guidance supports it. Wear protection, follow label rates exactly, and keep chemicals away from children, food, and water sources. Prefer non-chemical methods first when they work.

Symptoms: need chemical control

Possible causes: high pest or disease pressure

Solution: Use pesticides only with local approved guidance. Wear protective gear. Follow label rates. Keep away from children and water sources.

title: When to Contact an Agriculture Officer
content:
When should I ask an agriculture officer for help?

Ask a local extension officer when you are unsure of the problem, the damage is spreading fast, or chemicals seem necessary. Bring clear photos of leaves, stems, and the whole plant, and do not guess pesticide doses.

Symptoms: unsure diagnosis, spreading fast, chemical needed

Possible causes: uncertain or high-risk problem

Solution: Contact a local agriculture extension officer. Share clear photos of leaves, stems, and whole plants. Do not guess chemical doses.
